title: Local Kubernetes Clusters and kubectl Debugging: Quick Revision
summary: Quick revision notes on choosing between kind, minikube and k3d, how kubeconfig clusters, users and contexts work, switching contexts and namespaces, kubectl explain and dry-run, and debugging with port-forward and exec.

chapters.title: Local Clusters and kubeconfig Mental Model
points: Local cluster tools run a real Kubernetes control plane on your laptop for dev and testing; kubectl just talks to whatever API server kubeconfig points at
kubeconfig (default ~/.kube/config, override with KUBECONFIG env var or --kubeconfig) has three lists: clusters (server URL + CA), users (credentials), contexts
A context = cluster + user + default namespace; current-context is the one kubectl uses for every command
Every cluster tool writes a context on create: kind-<name>, minikube, k3d-<name>
KUBECONFIG can hold a colon-separated list of files (semicolon on Windows) that kubectl merges: kubectl config view --flatten shows the merged result

chapters.title: kind vs minikube vs k3d
points: kind = Kubernetes IN Docker: each node is a Docker container; built for testing Kubernetes itself and CI; multi-node and HA via a YAML config

minikube = single-node VM or container by default (drivers: docker, hyperkit, hyper-v, virtualbox); richest addons (minikube addons enable ingress, metrics-server, dashboard); --nodes N for multi-node
k3d = runs k3s (lightweight Rancher distro) in Docker; fastest start and lowest memory; built-in local registry (k3d registry create) and load balancer port mapping (-p 8080:80@loadbalancer)
Comparison: CI and multi-node testing → kind; beginners wanting addons and dashboard → minikube; fast, light, many clusters → k3d
Create/delete: kind create cluster --name dev / kind delete cluster --name dev; minikube start -p dev / minikube delete -p dev; k3d cluster create dev --servers 1 --agents 2 / k3d cluster delete dev
Local images are not visible to the cluster: use kind load docker-image app:1 --name dev, minikube image load app:1, or k3d image import app:1 -c dev, otherwise ErrImagePull

chapters.title: Contexts, Users and Switching Namespaces
points: List and inspect: kubectl config get-contexts; kubectl config current-context; kubectl config view --minify shows only the active context
Switch cluster: kubectl config use-context kind-dev; one-off override without switching: kubectl --context kind-dev get pods
Set a default namespace on the current context: kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=staging; per-command override with -n staging or -A for all namespaces
Users hold credentials (client cert/key, token, or exec plugin like aws eks get-token); two contexts can share one cluster with different users or namespaces

Gotcha: use-context persists across terminals, so running kubectl delete in the wrong context hits prod; check current-context first, use --context explicitly in scripts, or install kubectx/kubens (kubectx dev, kubens staging)

chapters.title: kubectl explain and Dry-Run
points: kubectl explain pod.spec.containers documents any resource field from the cluster's own API schema; walk down with dots; --recursive prints the whole field tree
kubectl api-resources lists resource kinds with short names, API group and whether namespaced (po, svc, deploy, ns)
--dry-run=client renders and validates locally without contacting the server; --dry-run=server sends it to the API server for full validation and admission without persisting
Generate YAML skeletons: kubectl create deployment web --image=nginx --dry-run=client -o yaml > web.yaml, then edit and apply
kubectl diff -f web.yaml shows what apply would change; mistake: forgetting -o yaml so dry-run prints only 'created (dry run)' and no manifest

chapters.title: Debugging with port-forward and exec
points: kubectl port-forward pod/web-1 8080:80 tunnels localhost:8080 to container port 80 through the API server (format LOCAL:REMOTE); also works for svc/web and deploy/web
port-forward is a debug tool, not exposure: it binds to 127.0.0.1 only, pins to one pod, dies when that pod restarts, and blocks the terminal (add --address 0.0.0.0 only deliberately)
kubectl exec -it web-1 -- sh opens a shell in the pod; the -- separates kubectl flags from the command; pick a container with -c name in multi-container pods
One-shot commands: kubectl exec web-1 -- env, kubectl exec web-1 -- cat /etc/resolv.conf; distroless images have no shell, so use kubectl debug -it web-1 --image=busybox --target=web
Debug order: kubectl get pods, kubectl describe pod, kubectl logs (--previous after a crash), then exec or port-forward; mistake: forgetting -n namespace and getting 'not found'

chapters.title: Cheat Sheet: Local Clusters, Contexts and Debugging
points: Create: kind create cluster --name dev | minikube start -p dev | k3d cluster create dev
Load image: kind load docker-image app:1 --name dev | minikube image load app:1 | k3d image import app:1 -c dev
Contexts: kubectl config get-contexts | use-context NAME | current-context | view --minify
Namespace: kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=NS | -n NS | -A
Explain/dry-run: kubectl explain pod.spec --recursive | create ... --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl diff -f f.yaml
Debug: kubectl port-forward svc/web 8080:80 | kubectl exec -it POD -c CTR -- sh | kubectl logs --previous POD
